cues.text: A Dispute Over Mary's Title
In 428, Nestorius , a monk from Antioch, became Patriarch of Constantinople.
He soon objected to the popular title Theotokos ("God-bearer" or "Mother of God") applied to the Virgin Mary, preferring instead "Christotokos" ("Christ-bearer").
Underlying the dispute over a title was a deeper Christological question.
Nestorius spoke of Christ in terms that seemed to divide him into two distinct persons, one divine and one human, loosely joined, rather than a single person truly God and truly man.

Nestorius's teaching reflected a broader theological tendency associated with the school of Antioch, which stressed the distinctness of Christ's human and divine natures partly to guard against blurring them together.
Alexandria, by contrast, tended to emphasize the unity of Christ's person so strongly that its theologians worried any talk of "two" anything in Christ risked dividing him.
The stage was set for a collision between two respected theological traditions, not merely between two personalities.
St. Cyril , Patriarch of Alexandria, saw in Nestorius's language a threat to the unity of Christ's person and, by extension, the Incarnation's reality.
If Mary bore only the human half of a divided Christ, he argued, God himself had not truly become man.
The whole logic of salvation was at risk.
Cyril appealed to Pope St. Celestine I , who in 430 condemned Nestorius's teaching and gave Cyril the authority to demand Nestorius's recantation within ten days or face excommunication.
The Council Convenes Amid Confusion
Emperor Theodosius II summoned a general council to meet at Ephesus at Pentecost, 431, hoping the assembled bishops would resolve the dispute.
Cyril and his supporters arrived in time; Nestorius came as well, confident of his position.
But John of Antioch and the bishops of the Syrian sees, who were expected to support Nestorius, were delayed on the road.
Rather than wait, Cyril opened the council on June 22, 431 with roughly two hundred bishops present, over the protest of Nestorius's remaining allies.
Nestorius, summoned three times to appear and defend himself, refused to attend.
His teachings were examined against his own writings and against Scripture, and the assembled bishops condemned and deposed him the same day.
Mary Declared Theotokos
When John of Antioch's delegation finally arrived days later, they learned that the council had proceeded and condemned Nestorius without them.
They convened a rival, much smaller assembly that in turn condemned Cyril—a split that briefly produced two competing councils claiming to speak for the Church.
Roman legates, arriving shortly after, sided firmly with Cyril's council and confirmed the sentence against Nestorius.
The council's central declaration affirmed that Christ is a single divine Person with two natures inseparably united from the moment of the Incarnation.
It affirmed that Mary, as the mother of that one Person who is God, is rightly called Theotokos , Mother of God.
The council also confirmed the Nicene Creed as sufficient and forbade the composition of any new, rival creed, and it renewed the earlier condemnation of Pelagianism.
Resolution and Aftermath
Theodosius II, faced with two rival councils each claiming legitimacy and each having excommunicated the other's leaders, initially had both Cyril and Nestorius placed under arrest.
Ultimately, the emperor recognized Cyril's council as the authentic one, and Nestorius was deposed.
His teaching was condemned as the heresy that came to bear his name, and he was eventually exiled to a monastery in Egypt, where he died some years later.
The controversy did not end cleanly.
Many bishops sympathetic to the Antiochene emphasis on Christ's two natures felt the council's condemnations had gone too far.
It would take the Formula of Reunion in 433, negotiated between Cyril and John of Antioch, to heal the breach between Alexandria and Antioch.
Those who continued to hold Nestorius's views split from the imperial Church altogether, forming what became the Church of the East .
Legacy
Ephesus stands as the third ecumenical council and the moment the Church formally vindicated the title Theotokos.
The title would remain central to Catholic Marian devotion and the Church's understanding of who Christ is.
The ancient Marian hymn Sub Tuum Praesidium and countless later prayers and feasts trace their theological confidence directly back to the council's ruling.
Its insistence on the single personhood of Christ set the stage for the even more precise Christological definition the Church would need twenty years later, at the Council of Chalcedon .
The permanent departure of Nestorius's sympathizers into what became the Church of the East stands as the first lasting institutional schism following an ecumenical council's decision.
It is a sober reminder that resolving a theological question in one assembly does not guarantee the visible unity of all who had, until then, considered themselves part of the same Church.
